items.title: How to tell queue starvation from a deadlock
items.body:
The two priority queues (nextTick and promise microtasks) drain until empty. If code keeps adding to them, for example a `process.nextTick` that schedules itself again, the loop never gets to the timers phase, so no timer fires and no request is handled. But the JavaScript thread is busy the whole time, running those callbacks. So the process sits at 100% CPU. A **deadlock** is the opposite: things are waiting on each other and nobody is running, so the CPU is idle. The guide: the signature of starvation is "hung, but the CPU is pegged, and timers never fire" — as opposed to a deadlock, where CPU is idle.

Why the others are wrong:
- A starving process does not exit; it keeps running.
- Steady heap growth points at a memory leak, not at starvation.
- Locks waiting on each other is what a deadlock looks like, the case we are ruling out.

excerpts.quote: Both prioritised queues drain to empty. Recursion in either one means the loop never advances. A 10 ms timer, versus three ways of being busy:

The lesson isn't the milliseconds, it's that **all three look identical from outside**: the process is at 100% CPU, responsive to nothing, producing no logs, with a healthy-looking stack if you attach a debugger at the wrong moment. The signature of microtask/nextTick starvation specifically is *"hung, but the CPU is pegged, and timers never fire"* — as opposed to a deadlock, where CPU is idle.

items.title: Why C prints between the two timer callbacks
items.body:
B and D are two separate timer callbacks, even if they are due in the same tick. Node runs one macrotask callback, then drains the microtask queue, then runs the next callback. B runs and queues C (a promise handler). Before D starts, the checkpoint after B drains the microtasks, so C runs. Only then does D run. Hence B, C, D. The guide: "Microtasks are drained after *each* macrotask callback, not after the whole phase."

Why the others are wrong:
- Queues are not ordered by source position; C did not even exist until B ran.
- The timers phase does not pause for promises; the microtask checkpoint simply sits between callbacks.
- Timers due together are still separate callbacks; they are not merged.

excerpts.quote: after sync: microtask: [ E ] timers: [ B-cb, D-cb ] E runs: microtask: [ F ] ← E queued F, and the drain CONTINUES F runs: microtask: [] timers: [ B-cb, D-cb ] B-cb runs: microtask: [ C ] ← drained before the NEXT timer callback

The line to remember is **B, C, D** — not B, D, C. Microtasks are drained after *each* macrotask callback, not after the whole phase. Two timers due in the same tick are still two separate callbacks with a full microtask checkpoint between them.

items.title: Why await Promise.resolve() does not let timers run
items.body:
`await Promise.resolve()` puts the rest of the loop body on the **microtask** queue. The guide: "Both prioritised queues drain to empty." The microtask queue is emptied completely before the event loop moves to the next phase, and each chunk adds the next one right back onto it. So the loop never reaches timers or I/O, and they still starve. To really give them a turn you must yield to the *macrotask* side: `await new Promise((r) => setImmediate(r))` waits for the check phase, and the loop passes through its other phases on the way. Better still, the guide says, do not run long CPU jobs on the JS thread.

Why the others are wrong:
- Chunk size does not help; microtask yields never let the loop advance.
- Wrapping the loop in `readFile` does not change how microtasks drain.
- Each await still yields to the microtask queue; caching is not the problem.

excerpts.quote: Both prioritised queues drain to empty. Recursion in either one means the loop never advances. A 10 ms timer, versus three ways of being busy:

The escape, if you must do a long CPU job on the JS thread, is to yield to the *macrotask* queue — not the microtask queue: ```js // WRONG: never yields the loop, timers still starve await Promise.resolve(); // RIGHT: yields to the check phase, letting timers and I/O run await new Promise((r) => setImmediate(r));

items.title: Why calling cart.checkout through a variable loses this
items.body:
`cart.checkout()` has a dot at the call: rule 3 (implicit binding) makes `this` whatever is left of the last dot, the cart. `const run = cart.checkout` does not call anything: `run` is just another name for the same function. `run()` then calls it with no dot in front, so rule 3 cannot apply and the call falls through to rule 4, the default binding. ES modules are always strict, so default binding gives `undefined`, and reading a field of `this` throws "Cannot read properties of undefined". The guide: most real bugs are "a call that fell from rule 3 to rule 4". Fix it with `cart.checkout.bind(cart)` or an arrow wrapper.

Why the others are wrong:
- Where the function was defined does not matter; the guide says "Not where it was defined. The last dot."
- `window` (globalThis) is the default only in sloppy scripts; a dot-less call in a strict ESM module gets `undefined`.
- Nothing is copied: `run` and `cart.checkout` are the same function, called without a receiver.

excerpts.quote: If the call has a dot in front of it, `this` is whatever is left of the **last** dot. Not the owner of the function. Not where it was defined. The last dot.
"Left of the last dot" is the phrase to keep — it explains the detachment bug later: `const f = obj.who` has no dot at the call site at all, so rule 3 cannot apply and you fall through to rule 4.
Ninety percent of real bugs are a call that fell from rule 3 to rule 4 because somebody moved the function where the dot did not follow.

items.title: Why static create should use new this(n)
items.body:
`class Dog extends Animal` wires two prototype chains. Instances of Dog delegate to `Dog.prototype` and then `Animal.prototype` (that is how methods are found). And `Dog` itself delegates to `Animal` itself, so statics are inherited: the guide verifies `Object.getPrototypeOf(Dog) === Animal`. So `Dog.create('Rex')` runs the base `create` with `this` set to the class it was called *on*: `Dog`. If `create` hard-codes `new Animal(n)`, it always builds a plain Animal, without Dog's methods. Writing `new this(n)` builds whatever class `create` was called on, so `Dog.create` gives a Dog. The guide: write `new Animal(n)` there "and you have silently broken every subclass."

Why the others are wrong:
- `Object.create(Animal.prototype)` still hard-codes Animal and skips the constructor.
- The guide's fix is `new this(n)`; `super` in a static points at the parent class, not the subclass.
- Statics *are* inherited through `extends`; redeclaring `create` everywhere is unnecessary.

excerpts.quote: Verified: `Object.getPrototypeOf(Dog) === Animal` is `true`, and `Dog.create` is inherited — a function, but not an own property. Which matters because inside a static method `this` is the class it was called *on*, not the one it was written in: `static create(n) { return new this(n); }` on the base correctly builds a `Dog` for `Dog.create()`. Write `new Animal(n)` there instead and you have silently broken every subclass.

Two chains, not one. **The top row**: instances delegate to prototypes — how methods are found. **The bottom row**: `Dog` itself delegates to `Animal` itself — how *statics* are inherited. `class B extends A` wires both edges, and the second one is the edge people forget exists.

items.title: Why the timer created inside a .then fires last
items.body:
During the synchronous run, two timers are registered: one that prints 2 and one that schedules a promise printing 4. Then the microtask queue drains and the `.then` runs. But it prints nothing; it only *creates a third timer* (printing 3). That timer joins the timers queue **behind** the two already there. Timers fire in the order they became due: 2 first; then the second timer, whose promise handler runs in the checkpoint right after it, so 4; then 3. The guide: "a promise handler confers no priority on the work it schedules."

Why the others are wrong:
- There is no extra clamp for timers created in microtasks; it is simply later in the queue.
- Timers keep their registration order; nothing reverses it.
- `setTimeout` callbacks run in the timers phase, wherever they were created; check is for `setImmediate`.

excerpts.quote: Sync first: `1`. Then the microtask queue drains, and here is the trap: the `.then` body prints nothing. It *schedules a timer*. So the only effect of the promise winning the race is that a third timer joins the queue — **behind** the two registered during the synchronous run. Timers queue: `[ prints-2, schedules-4, prints-3 ]`, in registration order.

The rule that doesn't help is line 3. "Microtasks run before macrotasks" tells you *when the `.then` executes*, not when the timer it creates executes — a promise handler confers no priority on the work it schedules. Timers fire in the order they became due, and a timer registered later is later, no matter who registered it. The general habit: track what each callback *queues*, not just when it runs.

items.title: Why an async function can still freeze the server
items.body:
`await` is not a pause button for the whole function. The guide: it is "return a promise now, and register the rest of this function as a `.then` handler". Everything *before* the first `await` runs synchronously, right where the function was called. In `buildReport`, `crunch(200000)` comes before the first await, so it runs on the call stack inside the request handler. Until it finishes, nothing else in the process can run, and the server freezes. Only `save(rows)`'s continuation is deferred. The guide: an async function doing expensive work before its first await "blocks the caller completely — the `async` keyword buys you nothing there."

Why the others are wrong:
- The body is not deferred; only the code after the first await is.
- `async` does not use another thread.
- The function runs at once when called; it does not wait behind timers.

So everything *before* the first `await` runs **synchronously**, right where you called it. Only the continuation is deferred.

items.title: Why .mjs and .cjs order nextTick differently, and what to rely on
items.body:
In CommonJS, top-level code runs as a plain script; when it ends, Node drains the nextTick queue first and then promises. An **ES module** is different: its top level is "evaluated as part of a promise job". So the microtask queue is already draining while your top-level code runs, and the promise callbacks you queued keep draining before the loop returns to the nextTick queue. That is why the same lines print promises first as `.mjs`. The guide says not to memorise top-level order. Learn the rule that holds **inside a callback**, where real code lives: nextTick, then promise, in both module systems.

Why the others are wrong:
- No loader sorts callbacks by name.
- Node does not run a separate event loop for ESM.
- nextTick is not disabled in ESM; it just runs after the promise drain at top level.

excerpts.quote: Both outputs are real, from the same eight lines. The reason: an ES module is *evaluated as part of a promise job*. The microtask queue is already being drained when your top-level code runs, so the drain continues before the loop gets back to the nextTick queue.
Do not learn "nextTick beats promises" as a top-level fact. Learn the rule that holds everywhere — **inside a callback**:
// logs: sync-in-timer → nextTick → promise (in .mjs AND .cjs)

items.title: Why a userland promise library shifts interleaving by one step
items.body:
`await` costs a different number of microtask "ticks" depending on what you await. The guide measured it: `await 1` and `await Promise.resolve(1)` resume after one tick, because native promises get a fast path in V8. `await { then: ... }`, a **thenable** (any object with a `.then` method, which is what a userland promise is), resumes one tick *later*: the engine must wrap it first, which costs an extra microtask. So after the swap, each await in that module resumes one tick later than before, and the order relative to another chain moves by one step, while every chain still finishes correctly. The guide: count ticks before assuming a bug.

Why the others are wrong:
- No await is skipped; the code just resumes later.
- Thenables still resolve through microtasks, not macrotasks behind timers.
- Awaiting always yields; nothing resolves synchronously inside `await`.

excerpts.quote: await 1 → >> resumed, tick1, tick2, … (resumes first: 1 tick) await Promise.resolve(1) → >> resumed, tick1, tick2, … (also 1 tick) await { then: … } → tick1, >> resumed, tick2, … (one tick LATER)

Native promises get a fast path (this was a real V8 change — older Node charged three ticks for `await promise`). A **thenable** — any object with a `.then` method — does not: the engine must wrap it, which costs an extra microtask. If you ever wondered why mixing a userland promise library into an async codebase subtly reorders things, this is why.

items.title: Concept: a stack, several queues, and a loop with phases
items.body:
Guide 01's opening says the short rule ("microtasks before macrotasks") is not enough to debug real problems. You need the actual machine.

The parts:

- **The call stack.** JavaScript runs one thing at a time. While a function is running, nothing else can.
- **Queues of waiting work.** Node has four lanes, not two: the `process.nextTick` queue, the microtask (promise) queue, and the *phase queues* of the loop (timers, poll for I/O, check for `setImmediate`, close).
- **The loop.** It walks the phases in order and runs callbacks from each. The two priority queues have their own draining rules, set out in the guide's section 2 diagram.

How to use this when reading a trace: write down, for every line, *which queue it puts work on*. Then walk the loop and drain the queues by the guide's rules. The guide draws the queue state at every step; copy that habit on paper. Most ordering puzzles stop being puzzles once you track what each callback **queues**, not just when it runs.

excerpts.quote: You can get a long way on "microtasks before macrotasks". You cannot debug a hung server with it, or explain why the same file prints a different order as `.mjs` than as `.cjs`, or say what `await` costs. Those need the actual machine: a stack, four queues with different draining rules, and a loop with phases.
The two-queue picture (microtasks, macrotasks) is enough for browser work. Node has four lanes, and they drain with different rules:

items.title: Why setImmediate always beats setTimeout inside an I/O callback
items.body:
The loop goes through its phases in a fixed order: timers, then poll (where I/O callbacks like `fs.readFile`'s run), then check (where `setImmediate` callbacks run), then round again. Inside a `readFile` callback you are already *in* the poll phase. The next phase is check, so the immediate runs there. The timer has to wait until the loop comes round to the timers phase on the next iteration. So the immediate always wins. At the top level of a file the order varies instead: `0` is clamped to 1 ms, and whether that has passed when the loop first reaches timers depends on how fast startup was.

Why the others are wrong:
- The guide explains the order by phases, not by a 4 ms clamp (the top-level clamp it mentions is 1 ms).
- `setImmediate` is not a microtask; it runs in the check phase.
- The callback runs on the main JavaScript thread, and `setImmediate` is never synchronous.

excerpts.quote: You are already *in* the poll phase, so **check** is the very next phase and the immediate fires; timers don't come round again until the next iteration. This is the concrete reason `setImmediate` exists: "run right after the current I/O, before any timers" is otherwise unsayable.

Both orders, repeatedly. The reason is a race against the clock: `0` is clamped to `1` ms, and whether that millisecond has elapsed by the time the loop reaches the timers phase depends on how long process startup took.

items.title: Why an arrow works as a callback but fails as a method
items.body:
An arrow function has no `this` of its own. Inside it, `this` is looked up in the surrounding code, like any outer variable.

- In `items.forEach(i => this.total += i)` inside a regular method, the surrounding code is that method. Its `this` is the object the method was called on, so the arrow uses it and works.
- In `const counter = { n: 0, inc: () => this.n++ }`, the arrow is written directly in an object literal at the top of a module. An object literal is not a function and gives no `this`, so the arrow uses the module's `this`, which in ESM is `undefined`. `this.n++` throws.

The guide's rule of thumb: "arrows for callbacks, methods for methods."

Why the others are wrong:
- Arrows never bind `this` to an object literal.
- `counter.inc()` cannot pass `counter` into an arrow; arrows ignore the receiver (and even `call` cannot change it).
- Object literals do not freeze anything; the problem is the arrow's `this`.

excerpts.quote: An arrow has **no `this` binding of its own**. Not "it gets the outer one at creation" — it genuinely has no slot, so `this` inside an arrow resolves up the scope chain like any closed-over variable. That is why none of the four rules

Rule of thumb worth having an opinion about: **arrows for callbacks, methods for methods.** An arrow as a callback is almost always right — it inherits the `this` you already have. An arrow as an object-literal method is almost always wrong: no enclosing method to inherit from, so you get module scope, which in ESM is `undefined`.

items.title: Start here: two long guides on the event loop and on this
items.body:
This pack uses two of the long-form essays in `guides/` of the jstrain2.2 JavaScript training repo. Every quiz comes from one of them.

Read in this order:

- **guides/README.md**: what the guides are for, the index (each guide says "read when..."), and "How they're built".
- **guides/01-the-event-loop-all-the-way-down.md**: the stack, Node's four queues, the loop's phases, six worked traces, starvation, and production consequences.
- **guides/02-this-prototypes-and-what-new-does.md**: the rules that decide `this`, how prototypes and `class` really work, and what `new` does.

Every guide has the same skeleton: a hook, numbered sections with diagrams, **Now go do** (bootcamp exercises that drill the ideas) and a **Self-test**. The README is blunt about the exercises: reading without doing them "is entertainment, not learning".

These guides are dense. Read one section, then run its code in Node (both as a `.cjs` and an `.mjs` file where the guide says it matters) before moving on.

items.title: What new does to a bound function and its bound argument
items.body:
`new` is rule 1, the highest priority: it creates a fresh object and makes it `this`, even for a function made with `bind`. So the bound receiver `{ ignored: true }` is thrown away. But bound **arguments** are kept: `P.bind(..., 1)` fixed `x` to 1, and `new P1(2)` supplies `y = 2`. The result is a new object `{ x: 1, y: 2 }`. The guide shows exactly this: `JSON.stringify(new P1(2))` gives '{"x":1,"y":2}', and sums it up: "`new` discards a bound **receiver** but keeps bound **arguments**."

Why the others are wrong:
- Functions made with `bind` from a normal function can be called with `new`; no TypeError.
- The bound argument 1 is kept, so x is 1 and y is 2.
- bind does not outrank new; the guide says "new beats bind".

excerpts.quote: `new` builds a fresh object and makes it `this`, and it outranks everything — including a `bind` that came first:

function P(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } const P1 = P.bind({ ignored: true }, 1); JSON.stringify(new P1(2)); // => '{"x":1,"y":2}' ``` `new` discards a bound **receiver** but keeps bound **arguments**.

items.title: Why a rejection caught only in a later timer crashes Node
items.body:
`sendAnalytics()` is async and rejects. Nobody awaits it and no `.catch` is attached yet. Since Node 15 the default is `--unhandled-rejections=throw`. Node checks for unhandled rejections at the end of a microtask checkpoint, which happens long before a 50 ms timer can run. At that check the promise is rejected with no handler, so Node throws and the process exits with code 1. The guide's example shows exactly this: the timer line "never runs". Attaching `.catch` later *in the same tick* would be fine; in a `setTimeout` it is far too late. "Fire and forget" becomes "fire and crash".

Why the others are wrong:
- It is not just a warning; the process exits.
- It is not silent; the default mode throws.
- Node does not wait for future code to attach a handler; it checks at the checkpoint.

excerpts.quote: **Unhandled rejections crash the process.** Since Node 15 the default is `--unhandled-rejections=throw`: ```js async function boom() { throw new Error('nobody caught me'); } boom(); // ← no await, no .catch setTimeout(() => console.log('this line never runs'), 50);

The timer never fires. The process is gone. And the reason it's a *loop* topic: the rejection is detected at the end of a microtask checkpoint, so attaching a `.catch` later in the same tick is fine, while attaching it in a `setTimeout` is far too late. Either `await` it, `.catch` it, or hand it

items.title: Concept: this belongs to the call, not to the function
items.body:
Guide 02 starts with one sentence to keep: "`this` is not part of the function. It is part of the call." The same function body gets a different `this` depending on how it is called, because `this` is like an invisible argument that the call supplies.

The guide then gives four binding rules, checked in a fixed priority order where the first match wins: `new`, explicit binding (`call`, `apply`, `bind`), implicit binding (the receiver in a call like `obj.method()`), and the default binding. Learn the order from the guide's ladder, and what the default binding gives in strict-mode and module code. Arrow functions are treated as a separate case; read that section and note where an arrow's `this` comes from.

The second half applies the same "one mechanism" idea to objects: JavaScript objects hold a hidden pointer to another object, and `class`, `new`, `super`, `extends` and `instanceof` are all spellings of that mechanism.

When a quiz shows `this` misbehaving, find the exact call expression that runs the function, then walk the four rules in order.

excerpts.quote: > **`this` is not part of the function. It is part of the call.**
Checked in priority order, first match wins. That order is the whole rulebook, and it is worth memorising as a ladder rather than a list.

Same story one level down. JavaScript has no classes. It has objects holding a hidden pointer to another object and a lookup rule that follows it; `class`, `new`, `super`, `extends` and `instanceof` are five spellings of that one mechanism.
